EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had peaked with widespread Extreme Drought (D3) in early March 2026 generally dissipated or significantly improved throughout the remainder of the month. While the month began with an intensification on March 3rd that expanded D3 across counties like Carroll, Clinton, and Howard, a pattern of heavy rainfall triggered weekly improvements. By the March 31st update, Severe Drought (D2) and Extreme Drought (D3) had been completely removed from nearly all 17 previously affected counties.||This dramatic shift included the total elimination of D2/D3 conditions in a broad sub-region covering Warren, Vermillion, Fountain, Vigo, Parke, Montgomery, Boone, Clinton, Howard, Tipton, Hamilton, Madison, Delaware, Henry, and Randolph counties. By the end of the month, the only remaining vestiges of the winter drought were limited to the northern half of Carroll County and a small sliver of northern Tippecanoe County, which both remained in D2. In the eastern corridor, D3 conditions���which had been steady for months���were systematically trimmed back between March 10th and March 24th before finally being removed.||Precipitation throughout March was exceptionally high for these areas, with totals ranging from 4 to as much as 9 inches. Specifically, western counties like Warren and Fountain saw deluge amounts of 9 inches, while the central corridor from Vigo to Boone received 6 to 8.5 inches, providing the necessary moisture to end the drought status by mid-month. Even in the more stubborn drought areas of the northeast, such as Delaware and Howard counties, monthly totals of 4 to 5.5 inches neared or exceeded double the normal rainfall, finally allowing for the termination of severe drought conditions. The remaining counties in D2 would see improvements out of severe drought in early April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D3 conditions at the start of the month for much of the county worsened on March 3rd to cover most of the entire county before heavy rains began to trim the D3 back down on the March 17th issuance and weekly afterwards through the end of the month. D3 drought ended on the 24th with D2 drought ending on the 31st. Rainfall amounts over the month were as much as 6 to 8 inches which allowed for the end of severe drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 26th daytime, temperatures were as low as -4F, while breezy winds were sustained up to around 15 mph...resulting in extreme wind chills as low as -24F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 10th, a discrete supercell moved from Illinois into northwest Indiana. It produced an EF-2 tornado in Starke County with maximum winds of 115 mph, prompting a rare Tornado Emergency for the area near Knox, IN. Training storms produced significant rainfall between 1 and 3, with localized amounts reaching 4-5, resulting in Flash Flood Warnings and Flood Advisories.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had peaked with widespread Extreme Drought (D3) in early March 2026 generally dissipated or significantly improved throughout the remainder of the month. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast moving system produced 3 to 6 inches of snow from portions of northwest Indiana into far northeast Indiana. Most of the heavier snow accumulation occurred roughly along a line from South Bend, IN to Fort Wayne, IN. The timing of the event produced moderate to high impacts for the morning commute.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bands of snow produced 2 to 5 inches of snow accumulation during the early morning hours of February 6th. Snowfall rates briefly reached as high as 1 to 2 inches per hour in association with the heavier bands of snow.  A public report of 4 inches of snowfall was received 1 mile south southeast of Rivare, IN. The morning commute was impacted with numerous slide-offs and accidents reported across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing theta-e, steep mid level lapse rates, strong shear and limited MUCAPE allowed for the development of several thunderstorms which moved from White county to northern portions of Allen county during the morning hours. Additional storms developed in the afternoon. Low freezing levels and the elements noted above resulted in efficient hail producing storms, with one in particular leaving a swath of 1 to 2 inches of pea size or larger hail along its path. A few severe level hail stones were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS observer measured at least one hailstone just over 1.5 inches in diameter.

While January had seen a significant degradation and expansion of drought intensity, February was characterized by a stagnant status quo, where meager precipitation totals prevented any meaningful recovery. Extreme Drought (D3) remained fixed across the north-central corridor, while Severe Drought (D2) continued to blanket much of the surrounding West Central and Central Indiana counties.||The most intense conditions remained centered on Howard County, which stayed entirely within D3 intensity throughout the month. This Extreme Drought also maintained its grip on much of Carroll and Delaware counties, the northern half of Tipton County, and the northern third of Madison County. Furthermore, D3 conditions remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County and northeastern Clinton County. Surrounding these areas, D2 conditions were maintained across the entirety of Warren, Tippecanoe, Fountain, and Vermillion counties, as well as the majority of Boone, Hamilton, and Montgomery counties. On the southern fringe of the drought���s extent, D2 intensity persisted in northwestern Parke, northwestern Vigo, and northern Henry counties.||Precipitation throughout February was once again critically low, frequently falling well below 50% of monthly norms. The driest conditions were observed in the northwest, where Warren County recorded less than a tenth of an inch of liquid equivalent, and Tippecanoe County saw only around 0.20 inches. Other hard-hit areas, including Carroll, Howard, and Delaware counties, saw totals struggle to reach 1.00 inch. While southern and eastern fringes like Henry and Parke counties received slightly higher totals ranging from 1.50 to 2.00 inches, the moisture was insufficient to overcome the long-term deficits. While D2 conditions were proscribed to end in March for several counties���including Vigo, Hamilton, and Boone���the drought remained firmly established for the majority of the region as the month concluded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation totaled only around 0.70 inches across the month of February. This maintained D2 conditions across southwestern Carroll county with D3 conditions across the rest of the county. These drought conditions continued into at least March 2026.

A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado tracked 4.10 miles over southern Sullivan County, between the Paxton and Carlisle communities. The maximum path width was 300 yards with multiple outbuildings significantly or completely destroyed and damage to trees.  The supercell originally spawned two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, which lifted before crossing the Wabash River into southwestern Sullivan County near Indiana Route 58. The tornado appeared to frequently come in contact with the ground at a few locations east of Route 58 but never remained in contact with the ground for a long distance, yet demonstrated damage that reflects high-end EF0 winds around 80 mph. The tornado maintained EF-0 intensity as it moved east-northeast through agricultural land, snapping a mix of large hardwood and softwood trees before lifting from Sullivan County. Damage was observed just northwest of Carlisle, where several small outbuildings sustained major damage. In this location, wind speeds were estimated at 80 mph, consistent with EF-0 intensity. The tornado continued across US-41 just south of Paxton, where the strongest damage, an additional outbuilding completely destroyed along with several large trees knocked over and snapped, was consistent with winds upwards of 85 mph;  the storm survey estimates that the width of the tree damage spanned around 300 yards in an adjacent field.  Peak wind speeds were estimated at 85 mph.

While ambient temperatures were not as deep into the negatives as previous events, a tightening pressure gradient across the region resulted in significantly higher wind speeds, which served as the primary driver for hazardous conditions.||West-northwest winds gusting to around 25-30 mph across central Indiana ushered in the cold by mid-morning on the 19th, with ambient lows holding steady at mainly single digit degrees across the impacted northern and central zones. These intense breezes led to a primary period of criteria wind chills for several counties, including Warren, Montgomery, Clinton, and Tipton. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 26th daytime, temperatures were as low as -2F, while breezy winds were sustained up to around 15 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -21F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-phased system brought a combination of system and lake enhanced snow to northwest and portions of north central Indiana Saturday night into early Sunday morning followed by more organized lake effect snow showers late Sunday into Monday. This prolonged snow event coupled with gusty north to northwest winds lead to hazardous travel conditions and numerous slide-offs and accidents across favored lake effect snow region across northwest and north central Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of system and lake enhanced snow Saturday night into Sunday morning, followed by a more organized lake effect snow phase Sunday afternoon through midday Monday. Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 2 to 5 inches, with the higher amounts in this range across the northern part of the county.  In addition to the snow, north to northwest winds gusting to 30 to 35 mph resulted in some blowing and drifting snow along with periods of reduced visibilities. Numerous slide-offs were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail was covering the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January 2026's final week and February 1st, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  The cold outbreak's final embedded short wave plunged the farthest south, from the Middle Mississippi Valley on January 31st to the Carolina coast on the 1st.  Associated arctic surface high pressure centered over the Louisiana Gulf coast early on the 1st, extended its amplified ridge axis back over Indiana and into southeastern Canada, amid a weak surface gradient.  Resultant clear skies and light winds prevailed over central Indiana's remnant 5-10 inch snow pack from the January 31st late evening through daybreak on the 1st.  Temperatures fell generally as low as -5 to -15F with widespread resultant wind chills of -5F to -27F over the majority of central Indiana, with criteria wind chills limited to only Putnam, Hancock and Shelby Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 1st pre-dawn to early morning, temperatures as low as -17F, and light winds sustained under 5 mph...resulted in extreme wind chills as low as -27F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a period of active winter weather, much of central Indiana remained entrenched in a cold, arctic air mass as the 19th began. While ambient temperatures were not as deep into the negatives as previous events, a tightening pressure gradient across the region resulted in significantly higher wind speeds, which served as the primary driver for hazardous conditions.||West-northwest winds gusting to around 25-30 mph across central Indiana ushered in the cold by mid-morning on the 19th, with ambient lows holding steady at mainly single digit degrees across the impacted northern and central zones. These intense breezes led to a primary period of criteria wind chills for several counties, including Warren, Montgomery, Clinton, and Tipton. Wind chills fell to -20 to -25 within the 19th 0800-1100 EST period, with the most severe conditions observed in Montgomery County where the combination of single digit air and 25 mph sustained winds produced a -25 wind chill.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures on the morning of the 19th were as low as 4F, while gusty winds were sustained as high as 26 mph...resulting in extreme wind chills as low as -20F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 26th morning into the early evening, temperatures were as low as -4F, with sustained winds around 15 mph...resulting in extreme wind chills as low as -24F.  During the 26th late evening into the overnight, temperatures were as low as -3F, with sustained winds around 10-15 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -21F.  During the 28th pre-dawn and early morning hours, temperatures were as low as -8, with sustained winds around 5 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -20F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had resulted in Extreme Drought (D3) over north-central Indiana by late 2025 generally expanded and intensified throughout January 2026. While D2 and D3 levels were maintained from the previous month, a significant degradation occurred on the January 6th update, where D3 intensity expanded across the heart of the region. These drought conditions remained entrenched without improvement through the end of the month and continued into at least February 2026.||This status quo included a primary sub-region where D3 conditions expanded to cover the entirety of Howard County and much of Carroll and Delaware counties. Significant expansion of Severe Drought (D2) was also noted, moving to encompass the remainder of Clinton, Hamilton, and Vermillion counties. Meanwhile, D2 intensity was maintained across northern Henry County and northwestern Vigo County, with a small additional expansion into north-central Vigo. In the northeast, Tipton County saw an intensification as D3 pushed into its northern portions, while D3 remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County.||Precipitation throughout January for these areas was critically low, with many totals falling between 0.75 and 1.25 inches. Even in areas like Henry County, which received a slightly higher 1.50 to 2.25 inches, the moisture was not enough to warrant improvement. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm that brought Evansville's 2nd largest snowstorm on record impacted southwest Indiana on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing around midday. After a brief lull overnight, moderate to heavy snow developed with a second wave that continued into the morning hours of the 25th. A brief period of sleet had occurred as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the early evening hours. Between 7 to 14 inches of snow and sleet was observed with the lowest totals occurring in Spencer County, IN where the greatest mixing had fallen. ||Significant travel impacts occurred with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Emergency dispatchers fielded 653 calls in Vanderburgh County, IN with deputies and firefighters responding to dozens of traffic accidents and medical emergencies. Near Evansville at Boeke and Vogel, a 52 year old woman who was driving under the influence was stuck in the snow with a tire coming off the rim of their car during the early morning hours of the 25th. Gibson County, IN issued an Emergency Declaration in line with the state of Indiana, in addition to a travel warning. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow that led to travel becoming extremely dangerous. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, government closures.

A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky and into far southern Indiana, changing precipitation over to sleet for a short period of time in some counties. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow and sleet totaling 8 to 11 inches fell across Scott County.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drone footage from Cass County Emergency Management shows evidence of a tornado southeast of Lake Cicott. Dozens, if not hundreds, of trees were damaged by the brief tornado along with instances of property damage. The tornado appears to have begun over a wooded area near the termination of S CR 750 W (South of W CR 50 S). Here, a few trees were uprooted followed by an area of trees snapped near the base. Based on a convergent signature, the tornado appears to have curved quickly to the northeast, taking a few roof panels off a nearby outbuilding. Now approaching the bend in the road of W CR 50 S, the tornado appears to have intensified sharply with intense destruction and uprooting of trees, resulting in a clear convergent pattern. Nearby buildings appear to have avoided significant damage. On yet another sharp jaunt to the north, now headed to a farmstead, the tornado continued to destroy trees but also destroyed two barns, removed portions of roof off three other outbuildings, and completely destroyed a grain bin. Debris was gathered at the base of a nearby tree line. Aloft, a few large branches appear to have been snapped. Beyond this, trees are untouched suggesting the tornado lifted.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on storm chaser and spotter photos and videos a brief satellite tornado developed just south of the primary and weakening tornado moving through Kouts. The location of this tornado is based on triangulation of the photos and videos. This tornado did not produce any known damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado developed in Dearborn County at 2314EST on Texas Gas Road, about 4 miles east of Dillsboro. It moved east and crossed Laughery Creek as  it entered Ohio County at 2317EST, about 2.8 miles southeast of Dillsboro. The tornado then moved across Laughery Creek, producing significant tree damage along and near Laughery Creek and in wooded areas along Hartford Pike, where numerous trees were snapped. Along Holmes Hill Road, more tree damage was observed along with the roof being lifted off an outbuilding. On Thuermer Hollow Road, more trees were damaged and a roof was lifted off a barn. Along State Route 56, additional roof damage to a barn and damage to large healthy trees were noted. Farther east on the Indiana side of the Ohio River, numerous trees were knocked down at a campground. The tornado crossed the Ohio River and entered into Boone County, Kentucky at 2325EST before it dissipated at at 2326EST, just across the Ohio River along Belleview Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first damage produced by the tornado occurred on Texas Gas Road, where a large tree was uprooted and other smaller trees were downed. Farther east along Cole Lane, an attached garage was destroyed and a large tree was downed onto a house. In addition, a roof was lifted from another garage and several trees were snapped at their trunks. ||The tornado strengthened and proceeded east near East Laughery Creek Road, where it completely destroyed a house and two outbuildings. Debris from these buildings was strewn east along the path of the tornado across a large field. Based on this damage, estimated wind speeds were around 130 mph in this area, and the damage also resulted in a Tornadic Debris Signature on the Wilmington, Ohio radar at this time. ||The tornado continued toward Alta Vista Ave, where a large number of hardwood trees were snapped. The tornado then moved across Laughery Creek and into Switzerland County at 2317EST, about 2.8 miles southeast of Dillsboro. The tornado continued east across Ohio County, eventually moving into Boone County, Kentucky, before dissipating at 2326EST, just across the Ohio River near Belleview Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 18th midday and afternoon hours, a fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms swept through central Indiana, producing widespread damaging straight line winds.  The severe weather entered the western portions of the IND CWA shortly after 1200 EST, with initial damage reported in Parke and Clay Counties where multiple trees and three power poles were downed.  The line tracked quickly eastward through the early afternoon, impacting the Indianapolis metropolitan area and adjacent counties. Widespread wind damage to trees and utility lines was noted, particularly across Owen County where an estimated gust of 55 knots (63 mph) downed a significant number of trees and powerlines. Further north, an estimated 60 mph gust in Boone County was followed by a measured gust of 53 knots (61 mph) at the Indianapolis Executive Airport north of Zionsville at 1335 EST.  Power lines were also downed in Hamilton County before the primary severe wind threat subsided.||In addition to the damaging winds, torrential downpours dropped widespread 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain across the region, producing significant areal and flash flooding from mid-afternoon into the evening.  Knox County was impacted first, where roughly 2.00 inches of rainfall caused water to flow over State Roads 58 and 67, flooded local intersections from Bruceville to Oaktown, and caused manholes to overflow. As the heavy rainfall progressed eastward, county-wide road flooding developed across Putnam, Hancock, Marion, and Owen Counties, with the latter reporting up to 3.00 inches.  The most severe hydrological impact occurred in Morgan County, where approximately 3.00 inches of rainfall inundated a residential home, requiring the deployment of sandbags to combat the rising floodwaters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and powerlines downed by thunderstorm wind gusts across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and early evening hours on May 16th, a Mesoscale Convective Vortex moved from west-southwest to east-northeast across the lower Ohio Valley, providing forcing for scattered showers and thunderstorms to develop. Thunderstorms were able to feed off of a seasonably high amount of instability, with around 2000 J/kg Mixed-Layer CAPE present in the pre-storm environment. While synoptic scale ridging over the southeast US meant that large scale flow was fairly weak, the MCV provided a mesoscale enhancement to the wind shear profile, with around 30-35 knots of effective shear supporting organized multicell clusters. Scattered strong to severe storms moved across southern Indiana, producing several reports of quarter sized hail and downed trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed along North Mill Street in Pekin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. On May 18th, storms which initially developed as scattered cells over southern Illinois merged into a line across southern Indiana. This line of storms had a modest amount of instability and vertical wind shear to support it, with temperatures in the upper 80s and dewpoint temperatures in the upper 60s supporting 1500-2000 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. Scattered wind damage was observed across southern Indiana, with the greatest concentration of damage occurring in Dubois and Washington County, where several trees were blown down. Additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms later in the evening would also lead to a few occurrences of flash flooding, especially along tributaries of the Blue River in Washington County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down at a home on Cedarwood Drive in Madison.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 19th afternoon, an unstable airmass ahead of an approaching surface trough triggered a cluster of severe thunderstorms across central Indiana.  Convection initially intensified over the western and northern portions of the Indianapolis metropolitan area shortly after 1500 EST, capitalizing on strong low-to-mid level wind shear. These storms quickly organized into severe segments that tracked eastward and southward, producing a concentrated swath of damaging straight-line winds across Hendricks, Hamilton, Delaware, and Bartholomew counties before exiting the IND CWA by 1700 EST.||Damaging winds were the primary hazard with this event, resulting in structural damage, power outages, and travel disruptions. Hamilton County was particularly hard hit, where estimated wind gusts up to 55 knots (63 mph) downed multiple utility lines, left a power pole leaning in Noblesville, and knocked a large tree through the roof of a residence.  Transportation infrastructure was also impacted:  in Delaware County, estimated gusts of 55 knots blew over a semi truck on Interstate 69 near mile marker 249.  Earlier in the afternoon, severe gusts in Hendricks County downed several trees, including one that blocked a roadway southwest of Danville.  As the severe weather pushed into south-central Indiana, the KBAK AWOS at Columbus Municipal Airport in Bartholomew County recorded a peak measured wind gust of 52 knots (60 mph).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utility lines down. Time roughly estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. On May 18th, storms which initially developed as scattered cells over southern Illinois merged into a line across southern Indiana. This line of storms had a modest amount of instability and vertical wind shear to support it, with temperatures in the upper 80s and dewpoint temperatures in the upper 60s supporting 1500-2000 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. Scattered wind damage was observed across southern Indiana, with the greatest concentration of damage occurring in Dubois and Washington County, where several trees were blown down. Additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms later in the evening would also lead to a few occurrences of flash flooding, especially along tributaries of the Blue River in Washington County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down along Indiana State Road 160 near its intersections with Franklin School Road and Conway Church Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. Given that the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, convection evolved into a quasi-linear convective system that moved across southern Indiana during the late evening hours on March 15th into the early morning hours on March 16th. The main observed severe hazard was wind damage from straight-line winds, with scattered damage to trees and power lines being observed across southern Indiana. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were down on Water Street in Salem.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of a cold front that produced widespread 60 mph wind gusts and severe thunderstorms, lake effect snow developed. Periods of significantly reduced visibilities were noted well inland across portions of La Porte, St. Joseph, and Elkhart Counties across northern Indiana due to the combination of snow and strong wind gusts. Storm total snowfall amount were generally in the 2 to 5 inch range across these locations with locally higher amount closer to 6 inches closer to the Indiana Michigan stateline.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of periods of moderate to heavy lake effect snow and gusty winds of 30 to 40 mph led to significantly reduced visibilities at times along with slick road conditions. A CoCoRaHS observer 1.8 ENE of Granger reported 6.0 inches of snow. Outside of this specific location, snowfall amounts ranged from 2 to 4 inches. Numerous accidents and slide-offs were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Non-thunderstorm wind gusts caused damage to a carport in Sullivan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Clifty Creek, rose through minor flood stage late on the 4th in Columbus, which was amplified by additional isolated downpours during the afternoon that totaled mainly 0.10-0.50 inches.  Twelve homeless individuals and three dogs had to be water rescued from their encampment under the US Highway 31 bridge over Clifty Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.

On March 13, 2026, a potent late-winter occluded storm system tracked across the Great Lakes while slowly filling, from early morning at 985 mb in northeastern Wisconsin, to late day at 989 mb over the northern Lower Peninsula of Michigan.  The system's cold front crossed northern and northeastern portions of central Indiana from 1000 to 1230EST.||Both an earlier corresponding low-level jet stream axis and a later tighter surface pressure gradient crossed the region, promoting widespread gusty winds veering from southwest to west-northwest while gusting to 45 to 57 mph.  When these two features briefly overlapped following the frontal passage, through midday to early afternoon hours, and also coupled with increased boundary layer mixing under plentiful sun, isolated highest wind gusts reached 58-67 mph.  Winds subsided quickly through evening hours.||This unusually intense gradient wind episode for the central Indiana region included measured gusts of 58+ mph at seven reporting stations;  four reports from Tipton County to Delaware County of semi trucks traveling on north-south roads being blown over to the east;  and widely scattered tree, power line, and minor property (mainly roof) damage that was most prevalent in Delaware County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A non-thunderstorm wind gust measured 62 mph from the west at 1330EST by KOKK Kokomo Municipal Airport.  Previous to this peak gust, other non-thunderstorm gusts to 59 mph were observed during 1050-1056EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blocking Kiesler Road.

During the mid-to-late evening hours on March 22nd, a strong cold front dropped across the Ohio Valley, bringing a sharp drop in temperatures in addition to isolated strong to severe thunderstorms. During the afternoon hours, temperatures surged to near record levels in the mid-to-upper 80s, though dewpoint temperatures remained in the low-to-mid 50s. As a result, as the front moved into the region, instability remained relatively limited, with 500-1000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE present. The large dewpoint depressions did allow for unseasonably high amounts of downdraft CAPE, and a strong gust front combined with the cold front to produce 45-55 mph winds separate from thunderstorms across southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. Scattered cells did become strong enough to produce near-severe size hail across southern Indiana, with between half inch and quarter size hail reported across Orange, Washington, and Harrison County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel to quarter size hail was observed in the eastern part of Orange County, near the Rego community. In French Lick and Paoli, smaller hailstones covered the ground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: River flooding in northeastern Jackson County was exasperated locally by heavy rainfall during the overnight of the 4th-5th around 2.00 inches, with the East Fork White River later cresting at Seymour in major flood stage on the 5th evening. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. Given that the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, convection evolved into a quasi-linear convective system that moved across southern Indiana during the late evening hours on March 15th into the early morning hours on March 16th. The main observed severe hazard was wind damage from straight-line winds, with scattered damage to trees and power lines being observed across southern Indiana. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were several trees blown down and a roof blown off a small livestock shed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

Both occupants were found submerged in 8 feet of water west of the Tunnelton community near the intersection of Earl Road and Lawrenceport Road.

On March 13, 2026, a potent late-winter occluded storm system tracked across the Great Lakes while slowly filling, from early morning at 985 mb in northeastern Wisconsin, to late day at 989 mb over the northern Lower Peninsula of Michigan.  The system's cold front crossed northern and northeastern portions of central Indiana from 1000 to 1230EST.||Both an earlier corresponding low-level jet stream axis and a later tighter surface pressure gradient crossed the region, promoting widespread gusty winds veering from southwest to west-northwest while gusting to 45 to 57 mph.  When these two features briefly overlapped following the frontal passage, through midday to early afternoon hours, and also coupled with increased boundary layer mixing under plentiful sun, isolated highest wind gusts reached 58-67 mph. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Non-thunderstorm wind gusts around 1200EST downed numerous tree branches in Noblesville.

A quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) pushed across central Indiana producing widespread damaging wind gusts with significant tree damage and some structural damage. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 26, 2026, a potent cold front tracked across central Indiana, interacting with a warm and unstable airmass to trigger severe storms.  Severe thunderstorms developed rapidly, producing large hail and damaging wind gusts across northern central Indiana that downed trees and power lines, leading to over 1,700 power outages as residents dealt with the abrupt onset of hazardous weather.||Significant structural damage was observed, including a destroyed pole barn and a garage roof failure in Clinton County. While the environment supported supercellular rotation and prompted numerous tornado warnings, the only severe modes were straight-line damaging winds and large hail, with reports of 1.5-inch hail in Veedersburg. The convective activity gradually weakened as it progressed south of the I-70 corridor and encountered a more stable airmass, effectively concluding the active weather event for the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed by thunderstorm wind gusts onto a power line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree of unknown size downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

A powerful supercell thunderstorm tracked an EF-3 tornado across northern Newton and northwestern Jasper counties and another EF-1 tornado through northern Jasper County during the evening of March 10th. The EF-3 destroyed a number of homes and caused significant damage to many other homes, businesses, and infrastructure, especially in the town of Lake Village where two fatalities occurred as a result of the storm. Additional severe thunderstorms later in the evening brought one inch hail to northern Lake and Porter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A destructive EF-3 tornado with estimated peak winds of 160 mph impacted portions of Newton and northwest Jasper Counties, most notably the community of Lake Village. After forming and causing EF-3 damage in Kankakee County, Illinois, this tornado crossed into Newton County between W 800 N Road and W 900 N Road near N 650 W Road. Upon entering the county, the tornado destroyed multiple outbuildings and significantly damaged multiple homes. On N 600 W Road, multiple homes were completely destroyed with debris blown clear of the foundations, consistent with EF-3 caliber winds. Nearby forested areas had almost all trees snapped or uprooted with some trees remaining standing with only stubs of a few large branches remaining, likely due to extensive lifted debris. Multiple homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was destroyed along N 500 W Road and along and near N 400 W Road. As the tornado crossed US-41 into the south side of Lake Village, it widened to approximately 1100 yards while damaging the roof and canopy of a gas station and a nearby retail building. Further north along N 300 W Road, multiple blocks of homes had significant roof damage and almost all trees were uprooted or snapped. The tornado continued eastward into a wooded area near the Lugene Links Golf Course, where a continuous corridor of trees was entirely uprooted. As the tornado neared W 950 N Road and N 150 W Road, a few homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was completely destroyed. The tornado continued to produce damage to trees and outbuildings as it traveled northeastward through mainly rural portions of northern Newton County and northern portions of Roselawn. The tornado continued into Jasper County and dissipated shortly thereafter. It was on the ground for over 35 miles and, at its peak, spanned a half mile in diameter. The storm destroyed numerous homes and resulted in around a dozen injuries and three fatalities: one in Kankakee County and the other two near Lake Village.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. Widespread hail ranging from 1.25 to 1.75 inches was also reported across Randolph, Marion, Sullivan, Daviess, and Martin counties. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 62 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. Given that the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, convection evolved into a quasi-linear convective system that moved across southern Indiana during the late evening hours on March 15th into the early morning hours on March 16th. The main observed severe hazard was wind damage from straight-line winds, with scattered damage to trees and power lines being observed across southern Indiana. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a power pole and tree down and on fire on the 1100 block of Ridgewood Drive.

During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. Given that the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, convection evolved into a quasi-linear convective system that moved across southern Indiana during the late evening hours on March 15th into the early morning hours on March 16th. The main observed severe hazard was wind damage from straight-line winds, with scattered damage to trees and power lines being observed across southern Indiana. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blocking both lanes on the 7800 block of South 600 East.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 9th evening, a moist and unstable airmass across central Indiana interacted with an approaching upper-level disturbance resulting in severe thunderstorms. Thunderstorms initially developed in western and northwestern central Indiana after 6:00 PM EST before organizing into line segments that tracked eastward across the region through the late evening and overnight hours.||Strong straight-line wind gusts were produced by the severe thunderstorms. Peak measured wind gusts reached 61 mph at the Purdue University Airport in Tippecanoe County and 63 mph at the Indianapolis Regional Airport in Hancock County. The severe winds caused broad impacts across Tippecanoe, Vigo, Clay, Morgan, Hendricks, Hancock, and Johnson counties, primarily consisting of downed trees, large tree limbs, and localized power line damage that created temporary roadway obstructions.||Repeated convective activity and heavy rainfall totals between 2.5 and 4 inches subsequently impacted eastern portions of the area during the early morning hours of June 10. This heavy rain led to localized flash flooding across roadways in Decatur County, though no building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded. This severe weather event would be the second of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed many trees and a few powerlines near IN-44 near Cope Road and Old Moore Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines downed by thunderstorm wind gusts in the Lapel and Anderson areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scattered trees and utility lines were downed from thunderstorm straight line winds north of Bicknell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 29th into early July 2026, a stacked subtropical ridge built northward from the Mississippi Delta through most of North America's eastern half, with its center nearly stationary near the Tennessee Valley.  Corresponding surface high pressure aligned from the Gulf coast to New England promoted light to moderate southwesterly breezes into central Indiana which maintained dewpoints usually in the 73-78 degree range and daily high temperatures in the low 90s.  Resultant daily maximum heat indices were generally 100-109 degrees, with several, mainly central to southern central Indiana zones, reaching heat indices of 110-113 on June 29th and/or 30th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A stretch of excessive heat began on the 30th with a peak heat index value of 105F recorded at the Columbus AWOS. This event continued into July.

Corresponding surface high pressure aligned from the Gulf coast to New England promoted light to moderate southwesterly breezes into central Indiana which maintained dewpoints usually in the 73-78 degree range and daily high temperatures in the low 90s.  Resultant daily maximum heat indices were generally 100-109 degrees, with several, mainly central to southern central Indiana zones, reaching heat indices of 110-113 on June 29th and/or 30th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A stretch of excessive heat began on the 30th with a peak heat index value of 105F recorded at the Shelbyville ASOS.   This event continued into July.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 27th afternoon to early evening, a stationary west-east frontal boundary combined with a very moist column and forcing from a short wave trough over the Middle Mississippi Valley, to produce heavy to extreme rainfall rates over Sullivan and Greene Counties, and later Martin County.  Resultant flash flooding was considerable during the afternoon east of Sullivan through the Linton area.  Less impactful early evening flash flooding occurred in Martin County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme thunderstorm rainfall up to 5.00-6.00 inches in under 4 hours near Linton and Switz City resulted in flash flooding that washed out a culvert on County Road 1225 West.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 6th afternoon to early evening, a moist column combined with dynamic lift from an approaching cool front to produce numerous to widespread training thunderstorms over northern portions of central Indiana.  While most cells were generally sub-severe, isolated damaging winds were most organized in Warren County and most intense at the Muncie airport.  More noteworthy was the quasi-parallel nature of the approaching boundary to the moist conveyor's axis, which produced multiple roudns of heavy rain over several zones, and considerable flash flooding in portions of Warren County and Fountain County where up to an estimated 7.00 inches of rain fell. This severe weather event would be the first of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme thunderstorm rainfall from slow-moving cells produced flash flooding along Indiana Route 28 and into multiple homes west of West Lebanon.  The Redwood Creek river gage at Route 28, RCMI3, rose from 4.79 to 13.43 feet in 1.5 hours to 1945 EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado with path length of 10.53 miles and maximum width 75 yards traveled across mostly rural areas of northern Warren County. The peak winds were 85 mph with the tornado causing mainly sporadic tree damage with corn fields showing clear convergence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous roads closed due to flooding in Terre Haute and points to the south in Vigo County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm straight line winds in central Martin County near the EF0 tornado, uprooted or snapped several large tree branches and a few whole trees, from Dover Hill to the Shoals area.  Carport damage also occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm rainfall up to 5.00 inches produced flash flooding in central Martin County as far east as the Shoals area.  Water flowed over several roads, including the confluence of Sherfick Stream and Gushing Creek onto Boyd Hollow Road, as well as Beech Creek onto Rama Dye Road where floodwaters where nearly 1,000 feet wide to the north of the creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 29th into early July 2026, a stacked subtropical ridge built northward from the Mississippi Delta through most of North America's eastern half, with its center nearly stationary near the Tennessee Valley.  Corresponding surface high pressure aligned from the Gulf coast to New England promoted light to moderate southwesterly breezes into central Indiana which maintained dewpoints usually in the 73-78 degree range and daily high temperatures in the low 90s.  Resultant daily maximum heat indices were generally 100-109 degrees, with several, mainly central to southern central Indiana zones, reaching heat indices of 110-113 on June 29th and/or 30th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A stretch of excessive heat began on the 29th with peak heat index value of 114F at Victory Field on June 30th. This event continued into July.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed numerous trees onto roads and power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 16th late afternoon and evening, a warm, humid airmass interacting with an approaching cold front and associated upper wave triggered scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Moderate instability and vertical wind shear promoted organized multicells and some supercells.||There were several severe hail reports, with diameters ranging from 1.00 and 1.25 inches impacting Carroll, Tippecanoe, Putnam, Hendricks, Marion, and Hancock counties. Straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts estimated between 58 mph and 60 mph also downed trees and large tree limbs across portions of Parke, Vigo, Putnam, and Morgan counties.||The primary severe event was a tornadic thunderstorm that tracked from Putnam County into western Morgan County. An EF-1 tornado touched down in Putnam County around 7:45 PM EST, with estimated maximum wind speeds of 105 mph. The tornado damaged several residences, destroyed an outbuilding, heavily impacted a mobile home, and snapped many trees. The tornado tracked along an 8.24-mile path across Putnam County before crossing into western Morgan County at 8:01 PM EST, weakening to an EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 70 mph. The tornado tracked an additional 1.13 miles causing minor tree damage before dissipating. The total path length was 9.37 miles. This severe weather event would be the fourth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with a total path length of 9.37 miles began at this location in Putnam County before crossing into western Morgan County where it dissipated. The maximum path width was 100 yards. The tornado moved mostly over rural areas causing significant tree damage, with a few structures also damaged. Significant damage occurred to a mobile home and two other residences were impacted. One barn was destroyed on one of these properties. The tornado may have skipped a few times along the path. Estimated max wind speeds were 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree uprooted, several limbs snapped by thunderstorm wind gusts.
