EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado with estimated peak winds of 95 mph touched down between W 700 S Road and Farrell Ditch, just west of S 500 W Road. The tornado damaged a barn and peeled shingles off of a house along S 400 W Road. Sheet metal from the barn was blown into a field several hundred feet to the east. Tree damage occurred as the tornado crossed Route 41. A barn was blown down and at least 5 utility poles were blown down as the tornado crossed S 200 W Road. The tornado turned northeast and blew the press box off of bleachers into a utility pole at a race track. The tornado was likely at peak intensity as it moved through the unincorporated community of Chase were a grain elevator and multiple associated grain bins were destroyed and a couple of tree trunks were snapped. The tornado turned east northeast snapping multiple rows of utility poles from Meridian Road to S 200 E Road and downing another set of power poles in Atkinson. As the tornado reached E 200 S and S 600 E Roads, it blew down more utility poles and a few trees. The roof, chimney and gutters of a house were damaged. A chicken coup was blown into a field, killing 30 chickens. The tornado ended just northeast of the intersection of E 200 S Road and S 600 E Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 9th evening, a moist and unstable airmass across central Indiana interacted with an approaching upper-level disturbance resulting in severe thunderstorms. Thunderstorms initially developed in western and northwestern central Indiana after 6:00 PM EST before organizing into line segments that tracked eastward across the region through the late evening and overnight hours.||Strong straight-line wind gusts were produced by the severe thunderstorms. Peak measured wind gusts reached 61 mph at the Purdue University Airport in Tippecanoe County and 63 mph at the Indianapolis Regional Airport in Hancock County. The severe winds caused broad impacts across Tippecanoe, Vigo, Clay, Morgan, Hendricks, Hancock, and Johnson counties, primarily consisting of downed trees, large tree limbs, and localized power line damage that created temporary roadway obstructions.||Repeated convective activity and heavy rainfall totals between 2.5 and 4 inches subsequently impacted eastern portions of the area during the early morning hours of June 10. This heavy rain led to localized flash flooding across roadways in Decatur County, though no building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded. This severe weather event would be the second of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree branch downed and shingles blown off by thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A strong long track tornado with estimated peak winds of 165 mph touched down in far southeast Lake County and crossed into far southwest Porter County where it quickly intensified. Widespread tree damaged including snapped and uprooted trees occurred along the entire path of the tornado in Porter County. Just east of Route 231 there was a swath of trees where nearly every tree trunk was snapped. Along S 625 W Road, a few farm outbuildings were destroyed and a house suffered roof damage. Several farm buildings, a garage and a manufactured home were destroyed along W 1000 S Road just west of S 500 W Road. Another house suffered major roof damage. A barn and farm outbuildings were destroyed just east of S 475 W Road. Farm buildings and grain bins were destroyed near S 350 W Road. Large trees were snapped and uprooted in this area. The tornado continued moving northeast and strengthened and widened as it moved north of Route 8. The tornado was likely at peak intensity as it moved across eastern Porter County. Several homes were destroyed and two separate sets of high-tension power trusses were sheared apart and collapsed. Significant scouring of the ground and crop damage also occurred. The tornado moved into LaPorte County just north of Slocum Ditch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 13th, a large trough of surface low pressure aligned from the central Plains to Ontario, combined with a very large surface ridge occupying the Deep South to the Atlantic Seaboard, to produce a strong surface pressure gradient across the Midwest.  Additionally, a small mid-level short wave trough, lifting from the Middle Mississippi Valley to the southern Great Lakes, induced a low-level jet stream over Indiana that produced 50-60 mph winds within 5,000 feet of the surface.  These very strong to marginally severe winds mixed down as gusts, including an observed 64 mph gust at the KIND Indianapolis Airport very early on the 13th.

Scattered thunderstorms moved across west central Indiana during the evening of April 27th producing isolated wind damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 21st, strong amplified high pressure along eastern North America promoted a robust surface gradient over Indiana, which produced southwesterly wind gusts of 25-40 mph through the afternoon to early evening. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Prolonged Extreme Drought (D3) had been present across much of far northern central Indiana, including most of Carroll County, since the January 6th 2026 update, with all of Carroll County and northern Tippecanoe County also falling into D3 between the March 3rd and March 17th updates.  All of these areas improved to Severe Drought (D2) on March 24th, with further improvement occurring on March 31st when the area of D2 decreased to only portions of Carroll County near and north-northwest of Camden, and extreme north-centeral Tippecanoe County.||This final patch of D2 across central Indiana's northern-most one percent, lingered amid very heavy rainfall of 2.20 to 3.60 inches during a one-week period through the early morning of April 7th.  The corresponding weekly update saw this area undergo a rare two-intensity-level downgrade to D0 (Abnormally Dry).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: April began with Severe Drought (D2) near and north-northwest of Camden, but following 2.20 to 3.60 inches of rainfall in only 1 week, on April 7th this area improved two drought intensity levels to Abnormally Dry (D0).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 2nd's early evening, an upper level short wave disturbance crossing the Middle Mississppi Valley, and associated 1000-mb surface low pressure tracking quickly from Iowa to Wiscomsin, placed central Indiana within its warm sector.  The conditional set-up for severe weather included steep 0-3 km lapse rates, and corresponding DCAPE values of 500-800 J/kg extending along and just east of the Wabash Valley.  A resultant quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) crossed western central Indiana, producing widely scattered damaging straight line winds.  The system's overall high cloud base mitigated any tornado production except where a brief EF-0 was spawned in Parke County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very brief EF-0 tornado dropped from locally lower ceilings within a bookend vortex embedded in the QLCS near Cecil Harden Lake, 1.3 miles southeast of the Hollandsburg community.  The bookend vortex crossed the lake, spawning the weak spin-up one-quarter mile south of the lake's southeastern shoreline;  along its 900-foot track, the tornado then crossed residential roads East Mallard Drive and South Ebert Drive, before ending 400 feet south of the lake's shore.||Drone imagery showed clear convergence of downed trees in a grove between Meadows Lane and Mallard Drive;  30 to 40 additional trees were either uprooted or snapped along the path.  Incident structural damage was limited to minor siding loss.  The tornado's damage was mainly vegetation, with peak ind gusts of 85 mph for the event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed an 18 inch tree.

South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 16th late afternoon and evening, a warm, humid airmass interacting with an approaching cold front and associated upper wave triggered scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Moderate instability and vertical wind shear promoted organized multicells and some supercells.||There were several severe hail reports, with diameters ranging from 1.00 and 1.25 inches impacting Carroll, Tippecanoe, Putnam, Hendricks, Marion, and Hancock counties. Straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts estimated between 58 mph and 60 mph also downed trees and large tree limbs across portions of Parke, Vigo, Putnam, and Morgan counties.||The primary severe event was a tornadic thunderstorm that tracked from Putnam County into western Morgan County. An EF-1 tornado touched down in Putnam County around 7:45 PM EST, with estimated maximum wind speeds of 105 mph. The tornado damaged several residences, destroyed an outbuilding, heavily impacted a mobile home, and snapped many trees. The tornado tracked along an 8.24-mile path across Putnam County before crossing into western Morgan County at 8:01 PM EST, weakening to an EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 70 mph. The tornado tracked an additional 1.13 miles causing minor tree damage before dissipating. The total path length was 9.37 miles. This severe weather event would be the fourth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of tree and structural damage along County Road 600S.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole with roof damage on Cody Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 6th afternoon to early evening, a moist column combined with dynamic lift from an approaching cool front to produce numerous to widespread training thunderstorms over northern portions of central Indiana.  While most cells were generally sub-severe, isolated damaging winds were most organized in Warren County and most intense at the Muncie airport.  More noteworthy was the quasi-parallel nature of the approaching boundary to the moist conveyor's axis, which produced multiple roudns of heavy rain over several zones, and considerable flash flooding in portions of Warren County and Fountain County where up to an estimated 7.00 inches of rain fell. This severe weather event would be the first of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.

Supercells congealed into a line of storms as it moved south into southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. These storms brought severe winds and a few tornadoes to the area. Additionally, long residence time of heavy rainfall lead to flash flooding that lasted through most of the day on June 18th, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Weather Service completed a storm survey and determined that a tornado occurred during the early morning hours on June 18, 2026 in Scott County and Jefferson County Indiana and then crossed the river into Trimble County Kentucky. The tornado was 1000 yards wide and 23.62 miles in length. Maximum winds were |EF2 130 mph.||The tornado first touched down on the northeast side of Austin, Indiana near the community park. Several trees were damaged with twisted tops or brought down entirely in the park. Some fencing and bleacher damage was also observed at the ball fields. The tornado continued across rural portions of Scott county just north of state road 256 with tree damage along the way. The most notable damage started occurring in extreme eastern Scott county north of Wooster along Blanton Road. Drone footage had shown a clear path in the woods of extensive tree damage with several house structures also having damage south of Hardy Lake. High end EF1 winds around 110 mph began here before the tornado crossed into Jefferson County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water flowing across multiple roads south of Terre Haute.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of storms occurred June 26-28th, 2026 resulting in significant flash flooding over southern Indiana and central Kentucky as well as an EF-0 tornado.  Several flash flood warnings were issued over the 2 day period with Considerable Flash Flooding in multiple locations and even Flash Flood Emergencies in some areas.  Rainfall totals for the weekend ended up in an area wide 2-4 inches with swaths of 6-10+ inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: East 6th Street from North Van Buren Street to North Cherry Street was flooded. Multiple vehicles were in high water.
